sentences.pattern: Crime prevention is most effective when + intervention + reduces both + opportunity + and + underlying risk.
sentences.cn: 当干预同时减少犯罪机会和根本风险时，预防最有效。
sentences.example: Crime prevention is most effective when street design reduces opportunity and youth services address underlying risk.

sentences.pattern: The perception that + place + is unsafe may persist even after + objective change.
sentences.cn: 即使客观情况改变，人们对某地不安全的看法仍可能持续。
sentences.example: The perception that a park is unsafe may persist even after reported offences decline.

sentences.pattern: Punishment can deter + behaviour + only if + condition of certainty/timing.
sentences.cn: 只有满足确定性或及时性条件，惩罚才能威慑某行为。
sentences.example: Punishment can deter offending only if people believe detection is reasonably likely.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: Prevention should combine environmental design with social support.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Reducing opportunities for crime is valuable, but durable safety also depends on addressing repeated risk factors.
writingIdeas.argument: Lighting, secure entrances and active street fronts can make offending more difficult and increase the chance of observation. These measures may displace rather than resolve harm if motivated offenders simply move elsewhere. Education, addiction treatment and stable housing address factors linked to repeated offending. No single programme works for every crime type. A balanced strategy uses immediate situational protection while investing in conditions that reduce future motivation and vulnerability.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: Public safety policy should distinguish crime rates from fear of crime.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Reported offences and residents’ sense of safety are related but require different evidence and responses.
writingIdeas.argument: A neighbourhood may become statistically safer while residents continue avoiding it because of poor lighting, visible disorder or memorable news coverage. Conversely, low fear does not prove that hidden domestic or financial crime is rare. Surveys, reports and local observation should therefore be compared. Communication must present trends honestly without dismissing personal experience. Effective policy reduces harm and enables people to use public space confidently, rather than treating either perception or recorded data as the whole picture.

speaking.question: What makes you feel safe in a public place?
speaking.answer: I feel safer when routes are clear, other people are present and I can see where I am going. Lighting matters, but activity matters too; an empty bright area can still feel uncomfortable. Reliable transport and visible staff also help because they provide a practical way to leave or ask for assistance.

speaking.question: Describe a change that made a place safer.
speaking.answer: A pedestrian tunnel near a station was redesigned after residents avoided it at night. The entrances were widened, damaged lights were replaced and the solid walls were partly opened so that people on the street could see into the route. A small kiosk was also placed near one entrance, adding ordinary activity through the evening. The tunnel did not become attractive simply because it was brighter; it felt safer because isolation was reduced and there was a clear view ahead. Local authorities continued collecting reports rather than assuming the design solved every problem. I noticed more people using the route after the change. It was a good example of safety emerging from several modest decisions rather than one dramatic security measure.

reading.title: When Better Lighting Does Not Reduce Crime
paragraphs: Improved street lighting is one of the most familiar crime-prevention measures. It can increase visibility, help pedestrians identify routes and signal that a place is maintained. Yet studies do not find identical effects everywhere. Light changes an environment, but the behaviour it influences depends on how that environment is used.

One theory is deterrence: potential offenders believe they are more likely to be recognised. Another is community activity. Better lighting encourages legitimate evening use, creating informal observation and stronger ownership. These mechanisms make different predictions. A brighter empty car park offers visibility without community presence, while a lit route beside open businesses provides both.

Measurement complicates evaluation. Police reports may rise because people can observe and report incidents more easily, even if actual offending falls. Crime may move to nearby streets, and seasonal changes can be mistaken for an intervention effect. Researchers compare suitable areas over sufficient time and examine several offence types rather than relying on a single before-and-after total.

Brightness can also create problems. Glare reduces the ability to see beyond a strongly lit area, poorly positioned fixtures invade homes and excessive light affects wildlife. Design should respond to pedestrian routes and actual risks instead of treating maximum illumination as universal safety. Maintenance matters because a failed lamp can leave sharper contrast than the original condition.

Lighting is therefore best understood as one component of place management. Its success may depend on sightlines, transport, building use and trust in reporting. A lamp cannot provide youth services or investigate violence hidden inside homes. It can support safer public movement when the mechanism is clear and results are monitored without claiming that every crime problem has the same visible solution. Community involvement can improve the diagnosis of place. Residents know where routes are avoided and when a nominally public area becomes controlled by one group. Their fear should inform investigation without automatically determining the solution. Combining local accounts with incident data and observation helps identify whether lighting, staffing, transport or a different intervention addresses the mechanism actually present.
